Hatchet started as part of the Y Combinator Winter 2024 batch with just an idea.
Both Hatchet co-founders had previously gone through YC S20 with different companies, Porter and Clearmix.
Hatchet got off the ground during the W24 batch with its first Hacker News launch.
Hatchet initially launched in early 2024 as an open-source distributed task queue built on Postgres.
Hatchet chose to build a platform bundling observability, alerting, replays and logging rather than a library.
Hatchet is fully MIT licensed with no enterprise edition.
Hatchet generates significant revenue from its cloud version.
Hatchet launched Hatchet v1, a full rewrite of the engine with new Typescript, Python and Go SDKs, in April 2025.
Hatchet did not release a new latest version in fall 2025 due to v0 removal cleanup after the October 1 deprecation deadline.
Hatchet grew cloud platform revenue 9x in 2025.
An engineer and an engineer joined Hatchet as founding engineers in 2025.
Hatchet made over 1k commits of bug fixes, performance improvements and smaller features in 2025.
Hatchet publishes weekly on The Hatchet Times.
Gabe and an engineer gave a Hatchet workshop at PyCon Sweden during the team's Stockholm offsite.
Community projects built on Hatchet include an unofficial Rust SDK and Scythe.
Hatchet's cloud offering runs more tasks per day than any known self-hosted instance.
Hatchet published a migration guide positioning itself as a replacement for FastAPI background tasks for production reliability and scalability.
Hatchet provides a dashboard showing task statuses and runtimes plus an OpenTelemetry integration.
Hatchet offers a hosted Hatchet Cloud service marketed as getting users running in five minutes.
Hatchet publishes content-marketing blog posts targeting Python developers, including one on Hatchet using modern Python.
Hatchet uses sqlc for writing SQL in its Go stack.
Because Hatchet is open-source and cannot assume user databases use connection poolers, it uses pgxpool for in-memory connection pooling.
Hatchet implements its job queue in Postgres using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
Hatchet found that batching Postgres writes can increase throughput by about 10x.
Hatchet's team had about two years of experience running Postgres in production at the time of writing.
Hatchet uses Postgres partitioning for historical task data.
The Hatchet founder was previously CTO at Porter, which managed deployments of hundreds of Kubernetes clusters into customer AWS accounts.
At Porter, the founder built an in-house orchestration system over several years, writing three versions of the provisioner.

After leaving Porter, the founder researched durable execution platforms, built an abandoned open-source Terraform automation project on Temporal, introduced Temporal as CTO of another company, and then started Hatchet.
Hatchet positions itself, like Temporal, as an external durable execution state store that persists workflow state and replays a durable event log on retry.
Hatchet markets itself for both durable execution and improved queueing workloads.
Hatchet built and shipped a terminal UI (TUI) for its CLI in about 2 days, mostly driven by Claude Code.
Hatchet considered building a new product line around terminal-based coding agents but decided against it.
Hatchet abandoned an agent-first refactor of its frontend that was built in a week and bug-bashed for five weeks, reverting the changes.
Hatchet did not really announce the TUI to its community, yet received unsolicited positive user feedback within days.
Hatchet positions itself as unique among orchestrators for supporting single tasks, durable tasks, and DAG-based execution.
Hatchet published a live demo of its TUI at tui.hatchet.run.
Hatchet runs on over 25 shards in 3 regions.
Hatchet's busiest shards run tens of thousands of transactions per second.
Hatchet adopted an 'andon cord' practice making shipping bottlenecks the overriding priority over new features and launches.
Hatchet paused work for 1 week to rewrite its entire deployment process after releases piled up.
Customers alerted Hatchet to latency before it knew, leading to a 2-week work pause to instrument critical-path endpoints.
Hatchet rolled out a new staging environment called staging-chonky and rewrote its load testing harness, pausing work for 1 week.
Hatchet says it shipped 3 new core engine features in one week after ramping up shipping velocity.
Hatchet provides much of its customer support through shared Slack channels.
Hatchet has a Discord community and a head of growth.
Hatchet's OpenAPI spec and codebase are public/open source.
Hatchet removed deprecated endpoints from its API after keeping them for a year following a major version increment.
Hatchet sometimes ships opt-in features to certain customers behind hidden docs pages.
Some Hatchet users self-host the open-source product.
Hatchet has observed coding agents placing unusual load on its API, including on undocumented and deprecated endpoints.
Hatchet released an idempotency keys feature, announced via a blog post on its site.
Hatchet used a long-form historical blog post about the origin of idempotency keys to promote its new idempotency keys feature.
Hatchet stores task payloads in Postgres using the jsonb column type, following a 'just use Postgres' approach.
Hatchet states a task takes less than an average of 25ms to be sent to the engine and start running on a worker.
Hatchet runs most of its hosted infrastructure on NVMe-backed Postgres.
Hatchet hit a scaling limit storing large amounts of jsonb payload data in Postgres, with payloads taking over 50% to 90% of database storage.
Hatchet's first WAL-based S3 offloading approach had problems with autovacuum pressure and S3 request costs, and was replaced.
Hatchet's write-and-swap approach offloads hundreds of millions of payloads to S3 each day and has run for a few months.
The 'supertoast' name was credited to Daniel Farina from Ubicloud.
Hatchet provides SDKs in Python, Go, and TypeScript.
Hatchet treats its SDKs as part of its frontend because they are usually a new user's first entrypoint into Hatchet.
Hatchet's Python SDK was rebuilt after the author joined, as the earlier version had sparse documentation and cryptic method names.
Hatchet designed its Python SDK to feel natural to FastAPI and Celery developers, positioning against existing tooling familiarity.
Hatchet writes all of its documentation by humans rather than AI.
Hatchet uses its blog as educational content, referencing posts from SDK warnings such as the blocked event loop warning.
Hatchet is a durable queue built on top of Postgres that stores up to hundreds of millions of tasks per day.
The first version of Hatchet stored runs in a single table, which bloated after reaching about 200 million rows.
Hatchet chose to build its own Postgres partitioning instead of using extensions like pg_partman or TimescaleDB so it could be deployed to any Postgres provider as an open-source project.
Hatchet v1 was essentially a rewrite of the entire Hatchet backend and bundled the new partitioning system.
After the v1 rollout, Hatchet had a production incident where queries on partitioned tables became up to 10x slower due to missing ANALYZE on parent tables.
Postgres expert an outside expert helped Hatchet debug the incident by suggesting manually running ANALYZE on parent tables.
Hatchet ships SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Go.
Hatchet's documentation was poor around the beginning of 2025, with SDK examples drifting out of sync.

time.label: Towards the beginning of this year

claims.statement: Hatchet experimented with LLMs to maintain documentation but abandoned the approach because generated code was unreliable.
Hatchet moved documentation examples into SDK repositories as tested code extracted via comment markup and published by GitHub Actions.
Hatchet says it has had no support tickets about broken documentation examples since launching the system.
Hatchet optimized its snippet parser from 2 minutes to 30 seconds runtime.
Hatchet plans to use LLMs to suggest prose updates for human review when code snippets change.
Hatchet was hiring engineers at the time of the post.
Hatchet states that the adoption of AI agents has been driving the growth of its orchestration platform.
Hatchet observed many of its users running hybrid stacks with a Next.js or FastAPI backend and an agent written in Go.
Hatchet published a blog post arguing Go is a good fit for building AI agents, positioning itself around agent workloads.
Hatchet describes itself as a platform for running background tasks, data pipelines and AI agents at scale.
Hatchet states blocked event loops are the most common problem it sees when providing support to users.
Hatchet's Python SDK runs synchronous tasks in a thread pool so they can execute in a non-blocking way.
Hatchet added a warning to its SDK to flag when the event loop might be blocked.
Hatchet's Python SDK provides an OpenTelemetry Instrumentor for exporting traces and spans from workers.
Hatchet uses Postgres as the backing database for its task queue, orchestrator, and monitoring system.
Hatchet spent half a year running hundreds of benchmarks against different Postgres configurations.
While scaling, Hatchet observed high CPU spikes, multixact errors, and high lock contention on its Postgres database.
Hatchet implemented lightweight in-memory buffers that flush batches of tasks to the database with backpressure.
Hatchet positions itself as a drop-in replacement for Celery that supports a modern Python stack.
Hatchet is open-source with a cloud version.
Hatchet's Python SDK drew inspiration from FastAPI and is Pydantic- and async-first.
Hatchet's Python SDK includes Lifespans (beta) and an OpenTelemetry instrumentor.
Hatchet has first-class cron support, removing the need for a tool like Celery Beat.
Hatchet uses its blog content, written by an engineer, to direct readers to try Hatchet Cloud.
Hatchet positions itself as a Postgres-backed task queue whose primary selling point is getting a powerful task queue by connecting to a Postgres DB.
Hatchet open-sourced its internal buffer implementation as a package called buffered.
Hatchet's step run events table on its largest database is at billions of rows with p90 latency of 100 milliseconds.
Hatchet uses TimescaleDB hypertables to store task success/failure metrics.
Hatchet offers a hosted product, Hatchet Cloud, alongside its GitHub open-source project.
Hatchet published the pg-events utility repository as companion content for the blog post.
Hatchet positions itself as a multi-language task queue with Python support aiming to be a drop-in replacement for Celery.
Hatchet's founders have migrated a number of Celery users to Hatchet.
A Hatchet co-founder published a blog post critiquing Celery as content marketing for Hatchet.
Hatchet uses a central engine plus a Postgres database for result persistence.
Hatchet supports Slack and email-based alerts on failure and has a UI for debugging and filtering tasks.
Hatchet described itself as an early project working on aggregate metrics views and dead-lettering support.
Hatchet gathers feature requests through its Discord community.
Hatchet implemented fair queueing strategies for Postgres-backed task queues in Hatchet and Hatchet Cloud.
Hatchet offers a managed version called Hatchet Cloud.
Hatchet used technical blog content with an open-source example repo (abelanger5/postgres-fair-queue) to explain its Postgres queueing approach.
Hatchet directs readers to its Discord for feedback.
Hatchet's fair-queue write approach achieves write throughput on the order of 500 to 1k tasks/second.
Cynco adopted Hatchet for its AI workflows to replace custom retry/wait workarounds and gain group round-robin fairness.
Cynco replaced an in-RAM FIFO Golang queue with Hatchet.
Hatchet can run with Postgres as the message queue instead of RabbitMQ for workloads under about 100 requests per second.
Hatchet offers SDKs for Golang, TypeScript, and Python, which the author contrasts with Python-only Prefect.
The author positions Hatchet as simpler than Temporal or Airflow, which need many dependencies.
Hatchet was part of Y Combinator's W24 batch and did a launch post on Hacker News.
Hatchet was founded by a co-founder and Gabe and positioned as a modern task queue alternative to Celery and BullMQ.
Hatchet's open-source repo is 100% MIT licensed.
Hatchet did an earlier Show HN a few months before the launch, when its cloud version was invite-only and focus was on open source.
Hatchet launched its self-serve cloud in the Launch HN post.
Hatchet was built out of frustration with existing tools and a conviction that PostgreSQL is the right choice for a task queue.
Hatchet published a blog post on problems with Celery.
After the Show HN, the most common ask was fanout workflows, so Hatchet launched child workflows.
Hatchet built webhook workers for HTTP-based triggers, useful for Vercel apps with timeout limits.
Hatchet launched hatchet-lite, a single Docker image bundling RabbitMQ and components, for local development and low-volume processing.
Hatchet was founded in 2023.
Hatchet was part of Y Combinator's Winter 2024 batch.
Hatchet is based in New York City.
Hatchet positioned itself at launch as an open-source, managed task queue alternative to Celery, BullMQ and Sidekiq.
Hatchet provides SDKs for Python, Typescript, and Golang plus a web UI and API.
At launch Hatchet was fully open source with an invite-only cloud offering.
Hatchet's founders are ex-CTOs of YC S20 companies: a co-founder of Porter and Gabe of Clearmix.
A co-founder started Hatchet after years of wrangling task queues and distributed systems at Porter and Oneleet.
Hatchet runs a public Discord for its community.
Hatchet now positions itself as an orchestration platform for AI agents, background tasks, and mission-critical workflows.
GetLatka estimates Hatchet's annual revenue at $440K in 2025.
Hatchet was founded by a co-founder, who is its CEO.
Hatchet had 4 employees in June 2024.
Y Combinator listed Hatchet with 2 employees in June 2024.
Hatchet is headquartered in New York, New York.
Hatchet was founded by the co-founders.
Hatchet's founders created it after dealing with background task management complexity as CTOs at companies like Porter and Temporal.
Hatchet is a platform for running background tasks built on Postgres.
Hatchet is positioned to help engineering teams build reliable applications, particularly in the AI space.
Dealroom lists a $125k seed round for Hatchet.
Dealroom states Hatchet has secured $500K in funding.
Hatchet supports applications written in Python, TypeScript, Go and Ruby.
Hatchet is offered both as a managed service, Hatchet Cloud, and as self-hosted software.
Hatchet is licensed under the MIT license.
Hatchet differentiates itself by using Postgres as a durability layer, making it easy to self-host.
Hatchet Cloud offers autoscaling and pay-as-you-go plans.
Hatchet positions its durable tasks as a drop-in replacement for Temporal or DBOS workflows.
Hatchet has been load-tested up to 10k tasks per second.
Hatchet uses Discord as its main community channel for contact with maintainers and contribution coordination.
The Hatchet README recommends signing up for Hatchet Cloud as the fastest way to get started, even for those planning to self-host.

company_stages.label: YC-backed idea-stage open-source project
company_stages.summary: Hatchet started in YC W24 with just an idea; repo created Dec 2023; fully open source with an invite-only cloud offering at launch.

company_stages.label: Open-source with self-serve cloud revenue
company_stages.summary: Self-serve Hatchet Cloud launched June 2024; MIT licensed with no enterprise edition; cloud generates significant revenue. Employee counts in June 2024 conflict between sources (4 vs YC listing of 2). Dealroom lists $125k seed and separately states $500K funding.

company_stages.label: Scaling cloud business with small team
company_stages.summary: In 2025 cloud revenue grew 9x, founding engineers joined, v1 rewrite shipped; GetLatka estimates $440K revenue in 2025. Later infrastructure runs 25+ shards in 3 regions and pay-as-you-go pricing announced 2026.

strategy_phases.label: Hacker News launches during YC
strategy_phases.summary: Early Show HN (Jan 2024) then a larger Show HN (Mar 2024) with focus on open source, followed by Launch HN for self-serve cloud in June 2024.

strategy_phases.label: Celery-alternative positioning and Postgres technical content
strategy_phases.summary: Positioned as Postgres-backed alternative to Celery/BullMQ/Sidekiq; published Celery critique, Postgres engineering posts, Python and FastAPI migration content.

strategy_phases.label: Repositioning toward AI agents and durable execution
strategy_phases.summary: Moved to describing itself as orchestration for AI agents, background tasks and durable workflows, and as Temporal/DBOS replacement; states AI agent adoption drives growth.

strategy_phases.label: Developer-experience and enterprise feature cadence
strategy_phases.summary: In 2026 shipped CLI, TUI, VSCode extension, OpenTelemetry, webhooks, enterprise/multi-team features, idempotency keys, concurrency features and pay-as-you-go pricing.

tactics.name: Launch on Hacker News repeatedly at product milestones
tactics.description: Use Show HN for the open-source launch, Launch HN for the cloud launch, and Show HN again for a major version.
tactics.mechanism: Each milestone gives a fresh reason to reach the developer audience.

tactics.name: Competitor-critique content marketing
tactics.description: Publish a post critiquing the incumbent tool your product replaces and position as a drop-in replacement.
tactics.mechanism: Captures developers already frustrated with the incumbent.

tactics.name: Deep technical engineering blog posts with companion repos
tactics.description: Write in-depth posts about internal infrastructure problems and publish example code/packages alongside.
tactics.mechanism: Educational content earns developer attention and credibility for the underlying product.

tactics.name: Migration guides from adjacent tools
tactics.description: Publish guides showing how to move from a common framework feature to your product.
tactics.mechanism: Lowers switching cost for users hitting limits of simpler tools.

tactics.name: Historical-story post to launch a feature
tactics.description: Promote a new feature with a long-form history piece about the concept.
tactics.mechanism: Narrative content travels further than a changelog.

tactics.name: Tested docs snippets extracted from SDK code
tactics.description: Keep documentation examples as tested code in SDK repos, extracted via comment markup and published by CI.
tactics.mechanism: Prevents docs drift; Hatchet reports no broken-example support tickets since.

tactics.name: Cloud-first README onboarding
tactics.description: Recommend signing up for the managed cloud as the fastest way to start, even for self-hosters.
tactics.mechanism: Routes open-source traffic into the revenue product.

tactics.name: Shared Slack channels for customer support
tactics.description: Support customers through shared Slack channels alongside a public Discord.
tactics.mechanism: Direct feedback loops surface feature requests and issues quickly.

constraints.name: Postgres scaling limits
constraints.description: Single runs table bloated around 200M rows; CPU spikes, lock contention; jsonb payloads took 50–90% storage; partitioning incident slowed queries 10x.

constraints.name: Open-source portability requirements
constraints.description: Must run on any Postgres provider and cannot assume poolers, so built own partitioning and in-memory pooling.

constraints.name: Documentation and support burden
constraints.description: Docs drifted in early 2025; LLM docs abandoned; blocked event loops are the top support issue.

constraints.name: Shipping and reliability bottlenecks
constraints.description: Work pauses to rewrite deployments and instrument latency after customers noticed; v0 cleanup delayed releases in fall 2025.

thirty_second.text: Hatchet is an MIT-licensed orchestration engine built on Postgres, with a paid hosted version called Hatchet Cloud. It started in Y Combinator's Winter 2024 batch, and its repository has grown to about 8,000 stars. The biggest jumps in stars came around the same time as the founder's Hacker News posts. Those included Show HN and Launch HN posts and deep technical posts about Postgres. The open-source README points new users to the cloud product, and the company reports that its cloud revenue grew 9x in 2025.

origin.text: A co-founder was previously CTO at Porter. There he spent several years building an in-house orchestration system and wrote three versions of its provisioner. He later researched durable execution platforms and built a Terraform automation project on Temporal, which he abandoned. He then introduced Temporal at another company before starting Hatchet. Hatchet was co-founded with Gabe a co-founder, the former CTO of Clearmix. The founders describe it as built out of frustration with existing tools and a belief that Postgres is the right base for a task queue. It entered YC W24 with just an idea, and the repository was created on December 15, 2023.

first_users.text: The first users appear to have been developers reached through Hacker News during the YC batch. A January 2024 Show HN got little response (7 points). A March 8, 2024 Show HN for an 'open-source distributed task queue' drew 578 points. That same day the repository gained 915 stars, within a 21-day run of 2,076 stars. At that point the focus was on open source, and the cloud was invite-only. Hatchet pitched itself as an alternative to Celery, BullMQ and Sidekiq, and the founders say they migrated a number of Celery users. The sources do not identify specific early customers by name.

flywheel.text: A plausible loop shows up in the evidence. The founder's technical posts and launches on Hacker News bring developers to the open-source repo. The README sends even would-be self-hosters to Hatchet Cloud, where the company reports significant revenue. Feedback from Discord and shared Slack channels shapes what gets built next. For example, fanout workflows were the most common request after the Show HN, so Hatchet launched child workflows. Each new feature or engineering lesson becomes another post, and star spikes followed several of these posts. The data shows timing only, so whether the posts caused the growth is not established.

did_differently.text: Hatchet chose Postgres as its only required dependency, so it can run on any Postgres provider. It built its own partitioning instead of relying on extensions. It also shipped a full platform with observability, alerting, replays and logging, rather than a library. The whole product is MIT licensed with no enterprise edition, and revenue comes from the hosted cloud. Its marketing leaned on detailed engineering writing about running Postgres at scale more than on product announcements. This reading is interpretive.

key_takeaways.text: Repeated Hacker News launches at milestones each lined up with a star spike. These came in March 2024 (Show HN), June 2024 (self-serve cloud), and April 2025 (v1 rewrite). The first launch attempt in January 2024 drew little response.
Technical posts about Postgres internals drew large Hacker News audiences, sometimes more than the product launches did. Examples include posts on multi-tenant queues and a Postgres survival guide.

Positioning narrowed against named incumbents and then widened. Early content targeted Celery and FastAPI users. Later Hatchet described itself as orchestration for AI agents and durable execution, and it says agent adoption has driven recent growth.
A fully open-source core sits alongside a hosted cloud that the README recommends first. Hatchet says this setup produced significant cloud revenue, including 9x growth in 2025.

Developer experience was treated as a growth input. Hatchet moved documentation examples into tested SDK code and reports no broken-example support tickets since. It also rebuilt its Python SDK to feel familiar to FastAPI and Celery developers.
